messages.subject: calculate SRMR for GGUM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I have a question about using the M2 function to calculate SRMR for GGUM. I know that you originally only allowed  to calculate SRMR for "dich", "graded", and "gpcm". But my coauthors recently found that SRMR works well for GGUM.

I used to be able to get SRMR for GGUM when I use the trace(M2, edit=T) to modify the function (add "ggum" to existing item types).  However, with the latest version (1.29), I am no longer able to do this. Do you have any idea? Is it possible to have this feature back?

Thanks a lot!

Best.
Bo

The first model (irt2) uses S-EM to estimate SEs; whereas, the second model uses the default Oakes method. The Oakes method does not produce any warnings, but the S-EM method states the warning below "could not invert information matrix; model is not likely empirically identified". Do you know why this might be happening? The call and output for each model are below.

messages.subject: Re: Linking without common items or persons
messages.subject_clean: Linking without common items or persons
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,

I'm not sure how to go about recommending a procedure to link items without somehow knowing prior information about the latent trait distributions. The purpose of linking is to effectively borrow common information across groups, and use this common information as a means to estimate a (hopefully) unbiased common metric. Without this, you would have to manually gauge how items should be linked, which requires you know something about both the latent trait distributions as well as the properties of the items.

For example, if you knew, based on outside knowledge, that one sample should answer items 1-3 with 50% chance, while the other group should answer the same items theoretically with a 60% change, then you have some information to at least link the metrics of the groups (thereby equating the latent trait distributions). But this feels like a stretch, and I'm not sure how you would know this. Alternatively, if you can assume that the latent traits across groups are identical theoretically, then the items are technically already equated and you can inspect items for DIF and other fun bias stuff. But again, this is a strong assumption, and likely untrue. Basically, you need to assume something about the items/traits before you can move forward. And that's something I don't have a lot of advice about. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
No, you could use the base M2() collapsing, which works quite well in most circumstances. C2 is a special variant when you run out of degrees of freedom in some models and only want to collapse the bivariate relationships rather than the univariate proportions into "scores") (the function in mirt is also broken on the current 1.29 version, so you should install the dev version on Github if you want the correction).

Phil

messages.subject: Re: calculate SRMR for GGUM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

Likert ratings are ordinal in nature despite the model we fit. For example, "strongly agree" should indicate higher degree of agreement than "agree".  Though the relationship between latent trait level and observed response it not monotonic in GGUM, it does not change the fact the the observed data itself is ordinal. Does it make sense?  I once asked Prof. Maydeu-Olivares and he also thought we could compute SRMR for GGUM as long as the data is ordinal.

Best,
Bo

messages.subject: Question about constrained GRMs and GRSMs
messages.subject_clean: Question about constrained GRMs and GRSMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil and everyone,

It feels like only the GPCM ("divide-by-total") family has a version constrained to items only varying in discrimination ("1PLish") with the Rasch Rating Scale.

Does it make sense / or is there any reason not to apply similar constraints in the "Graded" family?  For example, to use nested model comparisons to test if items vary in location (equal-slopes GRSM) vs. location + discrimination (GRSM) vs. location+discrimination+category structure (GRM).

It seems like it's very possible with mirt to do it (thanks for this!) from the item type "grsm", for example (for 6 items) :
mirt(data, item = "grsm", model = "G = 1-6 \n CONSTRAIN = (1-6, a1)" )

But since I hardly see it in the literature I guess I'm wondering if it's a big mistake to do it (or if it's just for historical reasons that it's rare).

Cheers,
Nils

messages.subject: Re: Question about constrained GRMs and GRSMs
messages.subject_clean: Question about constrained GRMs and GRSMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nils,

You certainly could apply those types of constraints and have similar benefits. From the statistical end, you improve the sampling variability of the model, so you typically get smaller SEs and other inferences when in fact all slopes are equal. I'm not sure if one obtains the so-called "objective measurement" properties Rasch-models often boast, but I imagine the total score statistics again become a sufficient source of information for estimating these models (don't hold me to that; I'm not sure if there's a proof of that anywhere).

In any event, I wouldn't consider doing such a thing invalid when the model fit does not get worse. But then, that's my same philosophy when it comes to the Rasch family as well (I'm one of those measurement people who don't hold Rasch models in god-like regard, particularly because they rarely fit the data well). HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the prompt reply! I completely agree with your "agnostic" perspective on Rasch models. :)
Nils

On Monday, December 3, 2018 at 1:54:08 PM UTC-5, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> Hi Nils,
>
> You certainly could apply those types of constraints and have similar benefits. From the statistical end, you improve the sampling variability of the model, so you typically get smaller SEs and other inferences when in fact all slopes are equal. I'm not sure if one obtains the so-called "objective measurement" properties Rasch-models often boast, but I imagine the total score statistics again become a sufficient source of information for estimating these models (don't hold me to that; I'm not sure if there's a proof of that anywhere).
>
> In any event, I wouldn't consider doing such a thing invalid when the model fit does not get worse. But then, that's my same philosophy when it comes to the Rasch family as well (I'm one of those measurement people who don't hold Rasch models in god-like regard, particularly because they rarely fit the data well). HTH.
>
> Phil
>
>
> On Mon, Dec 3, 2018 at 1:26 PM Nils Myszkowski <nilsmyszko...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Phil and everyone,
> >
> > It feels like only the GPCM ("divide-by-total") family has a version constrained to items only varying in discrimination ("1PLish") with the Rasch Rating Scale.
> >
> > Does it make sense / or is there any reason not to apply similar constraints in the "Graded" family?  For example, to use nested model comparisons to test if items vary in location (equal-slopes GRSM) vs. location + discrimination (GRSM) vs. location+discrimination+category structure (GRM).
> >
> > It seems like it's very possible with mirt to do it (thanks for this!) from the item type "grsm", for example (for 6 items) :
> > mirt(data, item = "grsm", model = "G = 1-6 \n CONSTRAIN = (1-6, a1)" )
> >
> > But since I hardly see it in the literature I guess I'm wondering if it's a big mistake to do it (or if it's just for historical reasons that it's rare).
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Nils

I was trying to estimate GGUM. However, the ML estimation give me some abnormal results (e.g., b1=-200). Therefore, I am thinking about assigning some priors to these difficult-to-estimate parameters.

When I only assign priors to taus, it worked. However, when I tried to assign priors for a1 and b1, I get the following error message.

Error: Error in nlminb(p, Mstep.LL, Mstep.grad, DERIV = DERIV, rlist = rlist,  :
  NA/NaN gradient evaluation

Here below is my code.

Model.CPS<-mirt.model("F1=1-9
            PRIOR=(1-9,t1,norm,2,2),(1-9,t2,norm,1,2),(1-9,t3,norm,0,2), (1-9, a1, lnorm, 0.2, 0,2)))")

IPM.F.E.Phy<-mirt(Data, Model.CPS,itemtype="ggum")

Do you have any idea what's going on?

Best,
Bo

messages.subject: Re: assigning priors to GGUM
messages.body_plain:
These errors are kind of frustrating because they are born from R's optim() function and difficult to prevent. I've tried over the years to minimize their effect and verboseness, but in the end I think it's impossible to do perfectly.

For more complicated likelihood spaces like those generated by the GGUM I would nearly always recommend using the optimizer = 'nlminb' instead of the default 'BFGS'. This optimizer is slower than the BFGS gradient-based family, but in my experiences seems to be more robust when the parameter space is difficult to work with. Let me know if you have any luck.

Phil

messages.subject: M2(..., residmat = T) doesn't output a residual matrix
messages.subject_clean: M2(..., residmat = T) doesn't output a residual matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

when fitting the following model:

expmodel1 <- mirt(data = MIRTdata[,3:49], model = 1, itemtype = 'Rasch')

...and then calling the M2 function:

M2(expmodel1, impute = 5, residmat = T)

...the function doesn't output the residual matrix, even though it was requested. My best guess is that this is because of the missing data and imputation involved (when trying out the same on one of the LSAT datasets, I got a residual matrix right away), but I'm still getting a SRMSR, which must have been computed from *something*. Find the data attached, although I've tried this with two other datasets (with similar levels of missingness).

Thanks a lot,
Adam

Phil

Hi Phil,

I tried to download the dev version of mirt using the instructions on your GitHub. I had version 1.29 and when I downloaded from GitHub, it updated to 1.29.8 (versus dev version 1.30). I’m not sure if I didn something wrong— but any advice on how to obtain dev version 1.30? Then I went back into R and used devtools (install_github('philchalmers/mirt'))to install and it was able to download an updated package but was not version 1.30.  After downloading, I used the C2 stat in the M2 function, and I’m getting negative CFI/TLI values so know my update is not correct.. thanks so much,

Keri

Phil

On Tue, Dec 4, 2018 at 3:55 AM <rico...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> I am using cross-validation in mirt:
> (1) Trained model: the model trained on one part of the sample and then
> (2) Tested model: the fixed parameter estimates from the trained model are tested on an independent part of the sample.
>
> I would like to evaluate fit on the independent sample using
> (1) M2: rmsea, tli, cfi,
> (2) M2: srmsr and individual item residual correlations,
> (3) personfit Zh,
> (4) itemfit S_X2.
>
> I computed the rmsea, tli, and cfi using the internal functions with the m2-statistic and the sample size (non-zero/non-perfect scores) from the test model and the degrees from the training model (correct?);

I don't really understand this part. What you should do is take the item parameter estimates from the training model and simply use these as the parameter estimates in the tested mode. Computing M2() on the new model should give some indication about the goodness of fit of the new data using old parameters, while the same approaches should work for all the other statistics as well.

> however, how shall I proceed to compute points (2), (3), (4) correctly?

In the same way as you would any other cross-validated model. Not quite sure what the issue is here, though perhaps you're thinking of something that I am not.

>
> Perhaps, a cross-validation function (or boosting) could be implemented in mirt in the future (I would certainly use it!)

Sure, but as you note what to look for in terms of validation is variable.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: cross-validation fit
messages.body_plain:
You're right, you should be using the df from the previous models. But in mirt, unlike some other software, it's easy to setup models to stop right at the starting values. Just pass TOL = NaN to mirt() and everything will terminate as is, where the new model will still have the same freely estimated parameters as your training model. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: why the loadings are negative?
messages.body_plain:
If the IRT model estimated is exploratory this behavior is expected. The models are rotationally indeterminate, so negative loadings will occur in the usual geometry. Confirmatory models are less likely to have these negative loadings, but they still are possible due to the fact that these are often partial coefficeints when items have more than one loading/slope.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: cross-validation fit
messages.body_plain:
Because M2 computes the collapsed moments based on the orthogonal compliment of the freely estimated parameters. Hence, you can't use the pars$est <- FALSE approach, because it's computing the M2 statistic based on parameters you are assuming to be fixed and known a priori. Other stats may not be this limited, but for the M2 you'd have to leave these parameters as estimated (i.e., your fit2).

Phil

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Dec 7, 2018 at 2:05 PM eaez <eay...@fordham.edu> wrote:
> Hi Phil!
>
> I have some questions related to this. I am also having negative slope parameters, in both general and specific factors in a bifactor model. Here are my questions:
>
> 1) Are negative slopes also ok in general factor of bifactor models (5 items out of 7 show negative slopes in the general factor)?

Sounds like the orientation got flipped somehow. Multiplying all slopes by -1 gives an equivalent fit, and solves your interpretation problem.

>
> 2) In general, which values of parameters are non-plausible in a bifactor model? Or alternatively, which range of values are more common in practice for the slope and intercept parameters? There probably is no hard-and-fast rule for acceptable parameter values, but I wonder if I should be worried if I have a slope parameter of say -3 or an intercept of 14.

Slopes past around 5 become essential step functions, which cause some pretty severe numerical problems during estimation (and for computing SEs). This applies to intercepts as well, but it's not really the values in isolation that matter but rather in concert. An intercept of 14 is only a problem when a medium-large slope is present, but with a 0 slope it's no issue at all. See my MBR article related to profile-likelihood confidence intervals for further details.

>
> 3) Are negative slopes ok in unidimensional 2pl or 3pl models as well?

If the majority are negative then flipping the signs is fine. Though having differing slopes in unidimensional models can be seen as problematic if the items are supposed to be measuring the same trait.

Phil

Thank you for your last response, it was really helpful. I have another question that I have been thinking about. To simplify presentation, I would like to marginalize score and SE for a bifactor model. What is your opinion on this procedure:

Theta <-expand.grid(seq(-6,6,0.1),seq(-6,6,0.1),seq(-6,6,0.1))
info <- testinfo(model, Theta, degrees=c(0,90,90))
SE <- 1/sqrt(info)

"We use estimated scores for each person j(gj,s1j,s2j,s3j,s4j) as sampled points on
the multidimensional grid to summarize high-dimensional information functions, in
the following manner. For each sampled point, item information functions will yield
scalar values; the TIF for the general factor can be easily computed by summing the
scalar IIF values. Finally, the standard errors can be computed and plotted against
estimated values of the general factor for all individuals in the sample."

Best,
Rico

This must be because you used na.rm=TRUE in the M2() statistic. Given your study design, removing cases row-wise no doubt removed so much data that the tables of counts were collapsed to only a single response option per item. Hence, computing things like correlations and covariances makes no sense if in the subset of data a single item has only the response 0-0-0-0-0-0-0....-0-0 an nothing else (zero variance).

> But these variables have three categories.

> "Moreover; once my model is estimated, the only way to compute fit indices such as RMSEA, CFI etc... is to impute the original dataset using the function imputeMissing ? Is this apporach correct ?
> Correct. I can't see any other way to do this because these statistics are based on complete datasets".
>

> Link here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/mirt-package/missing$20complete$20cfi%7Csort:date/mirt-package/slssi-7_koA/N-bghDqJBgAJ
>

That's correct. And the imputation approach that mirt uses is rather conservative. Multiple imputation from outside information would be better to help remove this issue, but that's an entirely different and difficult beast to tackle.

>
> The third question is related to different results between mirt estimation and ltm estimation. The correlation is negative (-.7) and I'm having a hard time to understand that.

> cor(coefs$items.a1,coefs$Dscrmn)

Simple, ltm didn't properly converge to the correct MLEs. This is a common and known issue with the ltm package that doesn't seem to exist in mirt (check out the log-likelihood values in your code, they are -15698.79 for ltm and -14606.65 for mirt....clearly, ltm got into a bad likelihood region and terminated wayyyy to early. And worse yet, without any warning). Here's a further discussion of the problem on CV: https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/63891/is-r-output-reliable-specially-irt-package-ltm/95324#95324

>

Hey Phil,

I believe I'm running into a case of bad item-fit and want to double check a couple things. First - a little context. I'm running data on 404 subjects on four different measures (ranging from 9 items to 54 items) all of which are measured on a 5 point likert scale. I've created thetas for each scale using the syntax I've pasted below:

GRM_Scale1 = mirt(data = Data,
                model = 1,
                GenRandomPars = TRUE,
                itemtype = "graded")

When I investigate item fit using S_X2 (Orlando and Thissen, 2000), some measures do better than others. For example, the 54 item scale only has one p value that falls below .05 - However, the results of a 13-item scale looks like the following:

      item   S_X2 df.S_X2 p.S_X2
1     itm1 54.408      33  0.011
2     itm2 45.867      26  0.009
3     itm3 57.335      27  0.001
4   itm4_R 48.283      37  0.101
5   itm5_R 79.100      48  0.003
6     itm6 34.629      26  0.120
7     itm7 27.304      23  0.243
8     itm8 62.454      42  0.022
9     itm9 57.816      38  0.021
10 itm10_R 47.448      34  0.063
11   itm11 22.479      18  0.211
12   itm12 27.968      26  0.360
13   itm13 24.276      25  0.503

Not so great, but with that in mind I have two question - One generic - One specific to mirt.

> 1. With respect to poor fit as illustrated above - Does the community have any recommended readings on the implications of using thetas derived from these analysis has on the confidence in the results.

My second question concerns using Stephen Stark's MODFIT program using the parameters generated from mirt. Specifically, I'm also trying to assess item fit using the singlets, doublets, and triplets statistic (X2 and adjusted X2) MODFIT produces (which I don't think can be done within mirt at this time). In order to run MODFIT, however, I need to provide item parameters (a, b1, b2, etc.). I believe that mirt deviates from tradition item parameters (but I'm not sure how) and in order to get traditional item parameters I need to include IRTpars = T in my code (e.g., coef(GRM_Scale1, IRTpars = T). So, my second question comes in two parts:

> 2. a) Is my assumption that mirt deviates from the traditional way of determining item parameters, correct (and if so, how)? and b) does the discrimination parameter produced by mirt include a scaling factor (i.e., do I need to divide a by 1.702 because MODFIT assumes that the discrimination parameter has not been adjusted in any way)?

Any feedback you all could provide me would be absolutely great!

Thanks,

Chris

That's a very complicated question, because it depends on the magnitude and direction of the misfit. Some thetas might be measured okay, while others not so much. It's difficult to give recommendations on this topic because there's an infinite number of ways items might misfit, and therefore an infinite + 1 ways that theta could be (mis)measured.

>
> My second question concerns using Stephen Stark's MODFIT program using the parameters generated from mirt. Specifically, I'm also trying to assess item fit using the singlets, doublets, and triplets statistic (X2 and adjusted X2) MODFIT produces (which I don't think can be done within mirt at this time). In order to run MODFIT, however, I need to provide item parameters (a, b1, b2, etc.). I believe that mirt deviates from tradition item parameters (but I'm not sure how) and in order to get traditional item parameters I need to include IRTpars = T in my code (e.g., coef(GRM_Scale1, IRTpars = T). So, my second question comes in two parts:
>
> > 2. a) Is my assumption that mirt deviates from the traditional way of determining item parameters, correct (and if so, how)? and b) does the discrimination parameter produced by mirt include a scaling factor (i.e., do I need to divide a by 1.702 because MODFIT assumes that the discrimination parameter has not been adjusted in any way)?

Yes, mirt estimates models using the slope-intercept form because it is more numerically optimal. Transformations can be done post-estimation as you have outlined. No, mirt doesn't include the 1.702 scaling coefficient.

I'm not familiar with the MODFIT program, but if you have references related to this program then it likely will be possible to write R code to do the same analyses without having to port between software (which is always problematic). Contributions like this are always welcome.

Phil

Cheers,

Chris

messages.body_plain:
MODFIT uses the Drasgow et al. (1995) X2 method. They do X2 tests for the n items individually but also for the n2 item pairs and n3 item triplets. This supposedly helps evaluate local independence of the items.

Drasgow, Levine, Tsien, Williams, & Mead (1995) Fitting Polytomous Item Response Theory Models to Multiple-choice Tests is the paper you want to find for all the details and math behind the method.

For model 1, is the model identified if you free the latent mean? I don't think that it is. messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reference (to you as well, Bo). This statistic looks interesting, and I'll spend some time formally reading over the paper, but my general impression after looking it over is that I don't see a solid foundation for statistical inference. Are the X^2 variates actually chi^2 distributed? It doesn't looks so, which is likely why the authors have done a X2/df correction to help reduce this effect, with the hopes that the expectations converge to the ratio 1 (which doesn't look to be the case). So, I'm wondering if this is just another approximate method, like the empirical theta estimate approaches to make similar goodness-of-fit tests (which I've commented in the past are not very good and problems). Basically, I'm wondering if this statistic has benefits over, say, the LD statistics that mirt already supports.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: [mirtCAT] reactive items selection
messages.body_plain:
It depends on how flexible an interface you are looking for. Yes, mirtCAT takes a lot of control away from the front-end developer to provide CAT control, which requires a lot of underlying statistical mechanisms. This is generally why I don't allow the server to be manipulated directly, though that could change in the future if there is enough incentive to do so.

At this time, I can't think of a fluid way to achieve what you are trying to do without a significant re-write of the server components. Sorry. It may be best just to write your own shiny applet and provide links to already running mirtCAT sessions, where each session corresponds to the desired topic.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: mixedmirt and estimation using EM Algorithm
messages.subject_clean: mixedmirt and estimation using EM Algorithm
messages.body_plain:
mixedmirt() currently only supports the MH-RM algorithm. Latent regression models can be run through mirt() though, but it sounds like you have an additional random effect structure to account for, so that likely is not applicable.

Regarding invariance tests, there are different styles of this but multipleGroup() is currently only for comparisons between two groups at a time, while mixedmirt() is more about conditional regression type models (where certain types of uniform DIF are possible, but the full-blown DIF approaches in IRT are generally not supported).

messages.subject: Re: Unidimensional vertical equating
messages.body_plain:
The colnames(U) part is telling mirt which items to treat as anchors, and therefore set the item parameters to be equal across all groups. This is required for equating because this is essentially what is assumed during the traditional equating process: the item parameters are equal (no DIF), and only different in independent samples because the ability parameters differ. Is this how you set your simulation code up?

Phil

messages.subject: 2 Questions: Subset of questions continuous responses and invariance specifications with n>2 groups
messages.subject_clean: 2 Questions: Subset of questions continuous responses and invariance specifications with n>2 groups
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I have two questions related to the best way to use mirt and IRT for my use case. I have a larger number of groups (n > 10) which all use different test forms with some overlapping questions.  The questions have a combination of binary, categorical and continuous response options. I want to use the multipleGroup() function for test equating.

My first question relates to how to deal with the questions that have continuous (or functionally continuous) responses (example: scale of 0-32).  Is it correct that mirt cannot deal with continuous responses? Are there other methods available potentially included in other software that could handle continuous responses? To solve this, I am currently dividing any item with more than 10 response options into quartiles and treating the question as ordinal categorical. For items with 10 responses or less I am specifying ordinal categorical without changing the scale. Is the 10 item response cutoff reasonable? Can you think of a better way of dealing with this without losing information from cutting the responses in quartiles?

My second question relates to the specification of anchor items and parameter invariance across a larger number of groups. An example of the structure of groups and questions is shown in the image attached. Sets of questions are wide and groups of individuals are long. Filled in blocks are where a group answered that group of questions, NA blocks are questions that did not get asked to a specific group. I understand that for the two group case, for questions that were asked to one group and not the other, I would want to specify the column names in the invariance argument, so that only one set of parameters would be estimated. However, how would you handle the three group case, where I want different parameters estimated for two of the groups (because there is evidence that the question functions differently between those two groups) but for the third group I don't really want any parameters estimated because the group was not administered those questions. Additionally, there could be a case in which all three groups are administered the same question and for two of the groups the parameters should be estimated as the same, but for the third group there is DIF and different parameters should be estimated. Ideally, instead of specifying invariance as column names, it would make sense if the specification could be a matrix that would tell you where parameter values could differ across groups and questions. Can you think of a way that I could handle this type of structure in mirt? If not possible in mirt, do you know of other software that would be able to handle this?

Thanks so much,
Emma
